title: Metrics for Agentic Systems: What "Good" Looks Like for a Security Agent
thesis: Activity counts such as runs, API calls and thumbs-up ratings do not show that a security agent improved security; a security agent should be judged on adoption, coverage, accuracy and ROI, with a separate safety gate, and the measurement itself has to be tested before the numbers are trusted.
summary: Najeeb works with Salesforce SOC analysts to build agents and automation. She opens with a security review where an impressive dashboard of runs, response times and thumbs-up ratings was met with the question of what actually improved. Her team went back and defined four lenses: adoption, coverage, accuracy and return on investment. Adoption is a fraction (18 of 40 intended users), and proving real use needs telemetry from ticketing and investigation tools: binding a recommendation ID to the analyst's approved action, comparing posted summaries to see whether they were edited or ghosted, and checking that a recommended query actually ran within ten minutes. Coverage asks which eligible cases, split by impact, the agent actually reached, and underpins the other lenses. Accuracy is split into recall and precision, the compounding loss across multi-step investigations (pass^k), and a study in which most correct final answers hid a missed step. She then asks who grades the grader and gives a ladder: state checks, code checks, a calibrated model judge and expert review of a sample. ROI is capacity value minus agent cost, and cost per reviewed correct outcome. A final safety gate covers authority, adversarial input and failure handoff, tested at intervals. The result feeds an expand, fix or keep supervision decision.
argument: Dashboards of runs, latency and thumbs-up ratings measure activity and sentiment, not security impact, and do not survive a basic question about what improved.

Four lenses answer that question: adoption (are people using the outputs), coverage (does it reach the work that matters), accuracy (which mistakes could hurt) and ROI (does useful work justify the full cost).
Each lens needs instrumentation that proves the claim, for example binding recommendations to analyst actions, rather than proxies such as ratings or impressions.
A single accuracy number can hide misses, lucky runs and correct answers reached by wrong steps, so the grader must be graded with state checks, code checks, calibrated judges and expert review.
A strong return cannot buy permission to skip a safety gate covering authority, adversarial input and failure handoff.
The combined evidence feeds a decision to expand, fix or keep supervision, made per action class and not per agent.

claims.claim: Adoption must be measured as a fraction of intended users with relevant work, not a raw count of users.
claims.evidence: Hypothetical example: 18 of 40 analysts used the outputs, giving 45 percent, and the 22 non-users are the group to study. The slide labels this a hypothetical example, not measured results.

claims.claim: Thumbs-up ratings and summary reads do not prove adoption; proof needs downstream telemetry from investigation and ticketing tools.
claims.evidence: Speaker's experience that adoption was the hardest lens to prove; three capture methods named: downstream action binding, grafted versus ghosted text diff, and execution of recommended artifacts.

claims.claim: A recommended action can be tied to a recommendation ID, and the ID is bound to the action when the analyst approves it, proving the analyst used the recommendation.
claims.evidence: Described as a design for recommendations such as blocking an IP or isolating a production domain; no deployment numbers given.

claims.claim: Summary adoption can be classed as edited (at least 80 percent of the agent text kept) or ghosted (analyst ignores it and writes their own), by diffing the ticket text.
claims.evidence: Definition with the 80 percent threshold given verbally; no measured split reported.

claims.claim: An agent's recommended SQL query or action counts as adopted if the exact query ran in the same system within the next 10 minutes.
claims.evidence: Stated as a method; no results shown.

claims.claim: Counting cases worked overstates coverage; coverage is cases reached divided by eligible cases, split by case type and severity, and skipped or untested work must stay visible.
claims.evidence: Hypothetical example of 45 distinct cases reached out of 60 eligible, 75 percent, with data fields to capture: case IDs, type and severity, delivered or skipped, skip reason and time window, tested situations.

claims.claim: An accuracy of 80 percent can hide precision of 67 percent: finding 8 of 10 true positives is 80 percent recall, but 4 extra false alarms drop precision to 67 percent.
claims.evidence: Worked hypothetical example; the slide adds a Wilson 95 percent interval of 39 to 86 percent on the precision count and notes small samples leave wide uncertainty.

claims.claim: Multi-step investigations lose accuracy as steps are chained, so a per-step accuracy must be multiplied across the run (the pass^k problem).
claims.evidence: Spoken example multiplied 75, 85 and 95 percent per-step accuracy; the slide illustrates independent trials at 75 percent each, where all pass probability falls to 56 percent at two, 42 percent at three, 24 percent at five and 10 percent at eight. Cited to tau-bench (Yao et al., 2024).

claims.claim: In a 240-trial study, 162 of the 175 runs that gave the right final answer had a process deviation such as a missed tool call or hallucinated number, so final output alone cannot establish accuracy.
claims.evidence: Cited study; the slide gives 92.6 percent and attributes it to an arXiv 2610.01833 (2026) reference. The speaker said 240 agent runs.

claims.claim: LLM-as-judge is unreliable because models tend to approve well-formatted output; the slide states tested LLM judges reached AUROC of 0.65 or less at detecting false success on tau2-bench.
claims.evidence: Speaker's own experience that a nicely formatted prompt gets a favorable grade, plus the slide figure; domain-trained detectors are shown at 0.83 on tau2-bench and 0.95 on AppWorld (2026 preprint, 11,755 runs).

claims.claim: A four-rung grader ladder gives more trustworthy accuracy: state checks, code checks on tool calls and arguments, a calibrated model judge with a per-dimension rubric that may answer unknown, and blind expert review of a sample.
claims.evidence: Method described and shown; no data on how the ladder performed in Salesforce production.

claims.claim: ROI is computed from capacity value (minutes saved times loaded analyst rate) against agent cost, and cost should be reported per reviewed correct outcome rather than total cost over total runs.
claims.evidence: Worked example: 100 cases, 6 minutes with the agent versus 10 without, 400 minutes saved, agent cost 100 dollars, analyst rate 60 dollars per hour, ROI about 300 percent. Slide formulas match.

claims.claim: More spend does not mean more accuracy: in a 21,730-run study, higher reasoning effort lowered accuracy in most runs.
claims.evidence: Cited on the ROI slide only; the study is not named and was not discussed aloud.

claims.claim: Repeated and adapted attacks raise hijack success: against one agent, tailored attacks lifted success from 11 to 81 percent, and 25 attempts lifted it from 57 to 80 percent (NIST CAISI).
claims.evidence: Slide figures attributed to NIST CAISI; the speaker only said agents must be tested for prompt injection.

frameworks.name: Four lenses plus a safety gate
frameworks.description: Adoption (are people using the outputs), coverage (does it reach the work that matters), accuracy (which mistakes could hurt us), ROI (does useful work justify the full cost), with a safety and reliability gate across all four.

frameworks.name: Five building blocks for measuring impact
frameworks.description: Task (what work should improve), Trial (what did the agent attempt), Grader (how do we check its work), Transcript (what evidence did we capture), Outcome (what actually changed).

frameworks.name: Grader ladder
frameworks.description: State checks (did the record, case or ticket change), code checks (tools called, arguments, order, policy rules), calibrated model judge (rubric per dimension, may answer unknown), expert review (blind to the agent's answer, adjudicate disagreements). Principle on the slide: test the checker with clean and deliberately faulted runs; models agreeing with models is not truth.

frameworks.name: Safety gate
frameworks.description: Authority (does a sensitive action need approval before it takes effect), adversarial (can untrusted alert data hijack the agent), failure and handoff (when a tool fails or evidence conflicts, does it stop and say so). Test before launch, after every model, prompt or tool change, and on a risk-based schedule; weight by impact.

frameworks.name: Expand, fix or keep supervision
frameworks.description: Expand when reviewed results and value support wider use, a tested scope and not the whole queue; fix when there is skipped work, recurring errors or avoidable effort; keep supervision when important evidence is missing. Decide per action class, not per agent.

frameworks.name: Adoption capture methods
frameworks.description: Downstream action binding (recommendation ID bound to the approved action), the text diff grafted versus ghosted, and execution of recommended artifacts.

slide_only: Slide 2 states five building blocks (Task, Trial, Grader, Transcript, Outcome) and that together the answers guide whether to expand, fix or keep supervision; the speaker did not say these aloud.
The adoption, coverage and missed-issue examples are labeled on the slides as hypothetical examples, not measured results; the speaker presented them as illustrations.
Coverage slide data to capture: all eligible cases and case IDs, case type and severity, output delivered or skipped, skip reason and time window, and tested situations with untested kept visible.

Accuracy slide has three panels: missed issues (80 percent found; 67 percent of warnings right, interval 39 to 86 percent), lucky runs (pass^k bar chart 75, 56, 42, 24, 10 percent at 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 trials) and process flags (92.6 percent). Sources line cites tau-bench (Yao et al., 2024) and arXiv 2610.01833 (2026), with Wilson 95 percent intervals on the hypothetical counts.

Grader slide: the figures 0.65 AUROC, 0.83 and 0.95, and the note that ExCyTIn-Bench and CyberSOCEval provide capability tests but do not establish a deployed workflow's performance, so integrations, permissions and outcomes need validating.

ROI slide shows three formulas: Capacity Value = (sum of (T manual minus T assisted) over cases / 60) times loaded hourly rate; ROI percent = (Capacity Value minus agent cost) / agent cost times 100; Cost per Reviewed Correct Outcome = agent cost / number of correct outcomes. Total attributed cost includes failed runs and retries.
ROI slide says report accuracy and cost together; in a 21,730-run study higher reasoning effort lowered accuracy in most runs.

Safety gate slide: tailored attacks lifted hijack success from 11 to 81 percent against one agent and 25 attempts lifted it from 57 to 80 percent (NIST CAISI); also 'Test the alarm', with a weighting rule that one severe miss outweighs many harmless ones.

Decision slide proposes: expand tested, reversible actions with limited impact; credential revocation, deletion and external notification stay human-gated; autonomy labels are shorthand. Closing line: state the evidence, name the next check.

quotes.text: A thumbs up rating is just polite sentiment rating.
quotes.speaker: Shahanas Najeeb

quotes.text: Looking at just the final output, we cannot determine the accuracy of the agent.
quotes.speaker: Shahanas Najeeb

quotes.speaker: Shahanas Najeeb

quotes.text: What if it decides to isolate a production domain without asking a human? Then this score drops to zero.
quotes.speaker: Shahanas Najeeb

offense: An agent could take an unsafe production action, such as isolating a production domain, without human approval; the speaker treats this as zeroing out all other metrics.
Untrusted alert data can hijack a security agent through prompt injection; the slide reports tailored and repeated attacks sharply raising hijack success.
LLM judges can be fooled into rating faulty runs as successful, so a self-referential grading loop can mask real failures.
defense: Bind each agent recommendation to an ID and tie it to the analyst's approved action to prove real use.
Diff ticket text against agent summaries to separate edited use from ghosted output, and check whether recommended queries ran within 10 minutes.
Measure coverage against eligible cases split by impact, and keep skipped and untested work visible.
Report precision and recall separately, grade each step of a run and not only the final verdict, and report intervals on small samples.

Grade with a ladder of state checks, code checks, a calibrated model judge with a rubric and an unknown option, and blind expert review of a sample; test the grader on clean and deliberately faulted runs.
Test authority, prompt injection resistance and failure handoff before launch, after every model, prompt or tool change, and on a risk-based schedule, weighting results by impact.
Decide expand, fix or keep supervision per action class: expand tested reversible low-impact actions, keep credential revocation, deletion and external notification human-gated.
takeaways: Replace run counts and thumbs-up ratings in agent reviews with adoption measured against intended users, using telemetry that binds agent output to analyst action.
Track precision and recall separately and grade the steps of each investigation, since correct final verdicts often hide process errors.
Do not rely on an unvalidated LLM judge; add state and code checks and a blind expert sample, and test the grader with deliberately faulted runs.
Report cost per reviewed correct outcome next to accuracy, not total cost over total runs.
Make expansion decisions per action class and keep a safety gate, with re-testing after every model, prompt or tool change.
limits: The speaker said fleet-wide evaluation is fragmented, with some teams using Salesforce Analytics and others using skills, and hopes for one unified platform in the next 6 to 12 months.
Small samples leave wide uncertainty, as the slide's 39 to 86 percent interval shows.
Adoption is the hardest lens to prove because no two agents are similar and telemetry must come from deep inside investigation and ticketing tools.
The slide notes that outside benchmarks test capability and do not establish performance of a deployed workflow.
critique: The adoption, coverage, precision and ROI figures are hypothetical illustrations; the talk reports no measured result from Salesforce production agents, so the effect of the framework is not demonstrated.
The talk opened with an account of a security review of a real agent dashboard but gave no before-and-after numbers, so the effect of the metrics program is not shown.

The multiplication of per-step accuracy (75, 85, 95 percent) assumes independent steps, and the slide's pass^k illustration is a different quantity (repeat trials of one task); the talk presented the two together.

The spoken statement that the 162 of 175 study covered 240 agent runs matches the slide, but the underlying study was cited only by arXiv number and the 21,730-run study not at all, so these external claims cannot be checked from the talk.
The ROI example prices only agent cost against analyst time saved and omits cost of review, false-positive analyst time and engineering upkeep, which the talk elsewhere treats as important.
The safety gate statistics come from a NIST CAISI result on a specific agent and are not tied back to the speaker's own agents.
qa: Leo (from the louis.ai team, as transcribed) asked what is bothering her as she looks ahead 6 to 12 months of evals. Answer: the agents are all over the place with no single place to measure metrics, some teams using Salesforce Analytics and others using skills; she hopes for a unified platform to evaluate agents as a whole.

An audience member asked whether professionals such as statisticians helped design the evaluations. Answer: the team did extensive research on how to measure accurately and arrived at the four lenses; once defined, getting the telemetry was not complicated and the metrics could be derived.

key_frames.caption: Adoption slide: the fraction framing (18 of 40) and the three capture methods, marked as a hypothetical example.
Accuracy slide: missed issues versus precision, the pass^k bar chart, and the 92.6 percent process-flag finding with sources.
Grader ladder and the AUROC figures showing LLM judges perform poorly at detecting false success.
ROI formulas: capacity value, ROI percent and cost per reviewed correct outcome.
Safety gate across all four pillars: authority, adversarial and failure handoff, with attack-success figures.

signal.reason: The talk presents a measurement framework with formulas and a grader ladder; the worked numbers are labeled hypothetical and the cited studies are named without detail.

caveats: Auto-captions garble some proper nouns; the Q&A questioner's affiliation was transcribed as 'louis.ai' and could not be confirmed.
The speaker's spoken job title was 'senior system design engineer'; the slide says Senior Agentic Security Engineer, Salesforce, and the slide is used.
Slides 09 and 10 of 11 were not captured, so any content on them is unknown; slide numbers 1 to 8 and 11 appear.
Spoken description of the 240-run study and the transcript's phrasing about pass^k differ slightly from the slide; the slide's 162 of 175 and 92.6 percent are used.
The 21,730-run and NIST CAISI statistics appear only on slides, and timestamps for them are approximate (the slide was on screen near those times).
Slide ROI percent: transcript says 100 dollars per hour for the agent, which the example treats as a flat 100 dollars of agent cost for the 100 cases.
